On the Run

By: Beth Neale | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A high-stakes, character-driven feature insert on South Africa's sardine run, told through the eyes of the netters who risk everything to chase a vanishing natural phenomenon.

Unique Selling Point:
1. Sardine Run Meets Human Drama
This isn't just another wildlife story. It’s a high-adrenaline, character-driven human story set against one of the greatest natural spectacles on Earth. The sardines are the hook—but the people chasing them are the real story.

2. Exclusive, Real-Time Access
The cameras are already rolling. We are embedded in the action with multiple crews and unprecedented access to the netters, skippers, and scientists. We've captured raw, real-time footage of chaos, danger, and victory—before anyone else.

3. Multi-Year, Multi-Perspective Coverage
We bring a deep archive of sardine run footage:

Inside bait balls in Port St Johns (freediving with sharks, dolphins, gannets)
Netting chaos from 2020 to now (boats flipping, ropes snapping, crates flooding the beach)
This year’s footage—sharks in nets, overturned vehicles, collapsing markets.
No other team has this combination of past and present visual storytelling.

4. The Story Behind the Spectacle
Most sardine run stories focus on the ocean. This story focuses on the people who depend on it—men and women gambling fuel, time, and safety for fish that might not come. It's blue-collar grit meets natural wonder.

5. Unfolding Economic Collapse
The sardine run economy is imploding in real time. Prices dropped from R1000 to R300 per crate in days. Netters are giving away fish. The audience gets to witness the collapse of a coastal economy—as it happens.

6. Urgency of a Vanishing Event
Scientists warn the sardine run may disappear by 2055 due to warming currents and ecological collapse. This may be one of the last great sardine runs—adding environmental urgency and journalistic relevance.

7. Diverse and Compelling Cast
From "The Sardine Whisperer" to the family of a drowned legend… from a father-son boat crew to shark-tagging scientists… and a diver who swims into shark-infested surf—the cast is built for storytelling.

8. Visual Style
Shot from the air, land, sea, and underwater, the project combines high-action GoPro, drone, underwater cinematography, and mobile footage. It's visually arresting, gritty, and immersive.



Summary:
Every winter, billions of sardines migrate up the east coast of South Africa in one of the greatest wildlife spectacles on Earth. But the real story isn't just underwater—it's on the beach, in the boats, and behind the nets.
On the Run is an immersive feature insert that captures the visceral chaos, the fierce rivalries, and the fragile economy built around the sardine run. It's a frontline story of fishermen who launch into pounding surf at first light, risking everything for a shoal that may never arrive. This is about more than fish. It's about survival, tradition, and timing. And it's already happening.


Further information:
Current Status: The sardines arrived early this year. Nets are landing—some full of sardines, others full of sharks. Vehicles have rolled on the sand. Tempers are flaring. Our cameras are already rolling. The story is unfolding in real time.
Our Focus: This insert will focus on the netters: approximately eight crews operating along the KwaZulu-Natal South Coast. These are small, competitive fishing teams who race against shifting currents, cold fronts, and each other to lay nets and get their catch to shore before the price crashes. Sardines sold for R1000 a crate on Saturday. By Monday, that dropped to R300.
And now, the economic model is breaking down. Yesterday, Rustin, one of the young netters, opened his net and let the public take the sardines for free. The market has already collapsed, and the season has barely begun. For many crews, the maths simply doesn’t make sense anymore. The financial future of the sardine run is as uncertain as the fish themselves.
We will place the presenter in the thick of it—launching with crews (only if the conditions are safe), hauling nets, walking the beach with skippers, and witnessing the chaos of a living, breathing economy built on the back of a fragile migration.

Press Release:


On the Run


The waters of the KwaZulu Natal coastline erupt as billions of sardines arrive – and the feeding frenzy begins. Birds dive, sharks circle, and the netting crews competing for the ultimate catch. They brave shark-infested waters, navigate dangerous surf, and
haul in heavy nets – all as tempers flare and tragedy hovers. This is a story of survival, tradition, and timing, set against the backdrop of a fragile coastal economy that lives and dies with the catch.

Script:


(Macfarlane) Every year, the greatest coastal migration on earth arrives in southern KwaZulu-Natal.



(Macfarlane) Billions of sardines travel up from the Cape, following a narrow band of cold water that only occurs in winter.



(Macfarlane) The predators are ready to feast.



(Macfarlane) Those on land are ready, too.



(Jace Govender) Let’s go! Pass the boat, let’s go!



(Macfarlane) Each winter, traditional netters chase the shoal, hauling in sardines during the narrow window they're in these waters. It's a job that vanishes when the fish do.



(Macfarlane) The risks - and the costs - are high. But so is the reward.



(Macfarlane) A single net can bring in R100 000 worth of sardines a day.



(Macfarlane) This is the sardine run and I’m joining the crews who chase fortune in every net they cast.



(Macfarlane) It's early morning and, as the sun comes up, there's only one question that lingers on everyone's mind along the coastline: where are the sardines?



(Macfarlane) One of the most well-known netters on the South Coast, Jace Govender scans the surf for any sign of sardines. He relies on his extensive network of spotters.



(Jace Govender) Keep your eye on it. I’m coming there. I’m launching now, now, now. Guys, guys, guys. Come, let’s go!



(Macfarlane) A spotter has seen a shoal close by. It’s game-on for Jace’s crew. He needs to launch his boat or lose out.



(Macfarlane) This is where all the action begins, right. As exciting as it may seem, it's also the most dangerous part.



(Macfarlane) It takes a seasoned boat skipper like Jace to make it through the surf.



(Jace Govender Subtitles) This is a game. It’s a cat and mouse game. You have to run around, drive up and down. Some days you get lucky, some days you don’t.



(Macfarlane) At first, it seems they’ve missed the shoal. Their luck is about to change. Time to lay the net.



(Macfarlane) Once it’s laid, the real battle begins - pulling tonnes of net and fish back to shore.



(Macfarlane Subtitles) Vans are getting stuck, people are falling over, it’s a mess. But it’s a wild and lovely mess.



(Macfarlane) Jace and his crew have struck gold, in silver.



(Macfarlane) Look! I caught my first sardine on the sardine run.



(Macfarlane) How long have you been doing this for?



(Jace Govender) All my life. I was born into it, I think, even before I was born, it was set for me to be a waterman.



(Macfarlane) Is it dangerous?



(Jace Govender) I think it's one of the most dangerous jobs in the world. You got the ocean to deal with. Two-tonne net, boat. Then you've got the sharks.



(Macfarlane) The sharks?



(Jace Govender) Yes, the big sharks.



(Macfarlane) Just how dangerous was demonstrated last year when our producers filmed veteran netter Goolam Essack hauling his final net.



(Goolam Essack Subtitles) I’m 74 now. I started as a 10-year-old boy.



(Unknown) For 65 years.



(Macfarlane) Tragically, Goolam’s boat capsized while netting and he suffered a fatal heart attack.



(Jace Govender Subtitles) Goolam is late, but his family's still into it. His son, his daughter, everyone. Goolam married my cousin. So, we’re family.



(Macfarlane) It’s a family affair.



(Macfarlane) But there’s little time to dwell on his family’s loss. Jace says that the sardine run employs up to 5000 people, and he has a full net to sell.



(Jace Govender) It's always a good day when you get the first net, because you’ll get the first buyers. So, you get the best price. The market can get flooded during the course of the day, but it also gives me a chance now to get a second net.



(Macfarlane) Once the fish are caught, there’s no time to waste - buyers want them fresh.



(Macfarlane) They’re packed into crates and sold, either to eat or as fishing bait.



(Macfarlane) That’s where Tony Moon comes in.



(Tony Moon) Hey! Bring all the fish here, guys!



(Macfarlane) With more than 50 years’ experience behind him, he’s one of the South Coast’s biggest netters and sardine sellers.



(Macfarlane) I see you are busy. It's like Tony's fish market.



(Tony Moon) Ja.



(Macfarlane) Do prices change throughout the day?



(Tony Moon) Yes, yes, yes.



(Macfarlane) Because I see, depending on…



(Tony Moon) You see in the morning, if only one guy nets, we can get a good price.



(Tony Moon) But when there's five netters netting and they’ve got full nets, then you know the guys are going to cut each and everybody's prices down.



(Sardine Seller) R20 a dozen! Three dozen, R50!



(Tony Moon) I started off here with R300, I went to R200 and now I'm selling R100.



(Macfarlane) And just like that, the coast goes quiet - not a sardine in sight. But they’re still out there. And so are the sharks. Lots of them.



(Macfarlane) The KwaZulu-Natal Sharks Board monitors shark activity along this coastline - especially during the sardine run.



(Macfarlane) Matt Dicken is their head of research.



(Matt Dicken) We monitor the sardines all the way from where they originate. And we track the movements up the coast to enable us to better predict the arrival of sardines so we can remove the bather protection gear, so we don't have mass captures of sharks and other animals in our gear.



(Macfarlane) The Sharks Board manages shark nets and baited hooks known as drumlines around popular beaches, aimed at lowering the incidence of shark attacks.



(Matt Dicken) So, when the gear comes out, the municipalities ban bathing.



(Macfarlane) During this time, it seems that there's more sharks than normal.



(Matt Dicken) The sardine run means a lot more sharks. When we talk about hundreds of thousands of tonnes of sardines, that obviously represents such an incredible food source not just for the sharks, but for a whole variety of predators.



(Macfarlane) We just heard that there may be a catch happening a few kilometres down. So, we are going to drive there and see what we can find. Sardine run!



(Macfarlane) This netting crew seems to be struggling with their catch.



(Jonathan Stamatis) Just got a huge net of fish that we can't even pull it up the beach!



(Macfarlane) Netter Demetri Stamatis is the conductor of this controlled chaos.



(Demetri Stamatis) Let’s move down slowly!



(Macfarlane) Driving the rhythm as his crew battles the net and the surf.



(Demetri Stamatis) Pick the sinkers up! Let it out!



(Macfarlane) This looks like a huge net.



(Demetri Stamatis) It’s a big net today. We had to let a lot of fish go. I think that’s about 350 crates or so.



(Macfarlane) Like Jace, Demetri has been doing this for a very long time. Decades ago, his father started netting from a rowboat.



(Demetri Stamatis) I got involved five, six years old, running around with him and… Ja, it's been in our blood ever since. And so my kids have got involved. So, I've got my two boys with me. So, three generations.



(Macfarlane) Three generations?



(Demetri Stamatis What more could we ask for here?



(Macfarlane) Your kids get in the water, they swim with the sharks. They’re pulling in those nets. Do you not sometimes sit there as a dad and think, “Oh, my God. I’m going to kill my son!”



(Demetri Stamatis) I don’t know. My dad made me do it, so I'm not worried about them doing it. I’ve been there and done that. But I won’t let kids jump into the surf when it’s not right.



(Macfarlane) Let's go, let's go, let's go! We’re making money, guys.



(Demetri Stamatis) Okay, I need to go.



(Macfarlane) All the best and thank you so much. Keep netting.



(Macfarlane) This is so exciting. I mean, while we are doing the interview, calls are coming in. The market is fluctuating. Seeing it happen in real time is mind-blowing.



(Macfarlane) Hold on, there’s a shark!



(Macfarlane) So, this is what we’re talking about, right? This is how far these guys are willing to risk their lives. They swim with the sharks.



(Macfarlane) It’s good news for Ryan Daly who tags and studies the sharks - including bronze whalers, dusky, spinner and blacktip sharks - drawn in by the sardine run.



(Dr. Ryan Daly) So, every year the sharks follow up the sardines and there’s so many millions of sardines, we can't really track them. So, we use sharks as our indicators of where the sardines are.



(Dr. Ryan Daly) The sharks are top predators and the sardines provide the biggest source of food for these predators on the whole coast. And so, sharks and sardines together play really important roles in the marine ecosystem. Sardines at the bottom of the food chain, sharks at the top of the food chain, keeping that balance.



(Macfarlane) In the chaos of the beach, Ryan performs open shark surgery, inserting a tag while battling waves, shouting crews and curious onlookers.



(Macfarlane) This year, over 20 sharks were caught in the nets in one day.



(Macfarlane) How does that impact then the sort of ecological system there?



(Dr. Ryan Daly) It's a really good sign, I think. So many sharks mean that there's a lot of sardines around. So, for me it's a good indicator that it's a strong run.



(Macfarlane) Once the sharks are released from the net, are they safe? Do you check if it's good to release?



(Dr. Ryan Daly) I've really experienced most of the netters caring about the sharks, making sure they're released safely. But we really don't know much about their survival after they get released. So, part of my question is to tag them after being caught in the nets to see if they do survive.



(Macfarlane) These guys risk life and limb with the sharks for the sardine run, but they set it free...



(Macfarlane) Ha, ha ,ha! Nice!



(Macfarlane) Sharks are stuffing themselves with sardines. I want a taste of what they’re after.



(Macfarlane) Are they fresh sardines?



(Rani Judnarain) Absolutely. They were caught today.



(Macfarlane) Did you catch them?



(Jace Govender) Ja, you were there! That’s my work.

 

(Macfarlane) I don’t mind eating food, but when it’s looking at me, it’s like, “Why are you doing this to me?”

 

(Macfarlane) After all the action, a bit of satisfaction, right?



(Jace Govender) This is the best form of protein.



(Macfarlane) I guess, at the end of the day, after all the hard work has been done and you get to enjoy a sardine on the beach at sunset, the risk is worth it all.

0000-00-00 Press Release: On the Run The waters of the KwaZulu Natal coastline erupt as billions of sardines arrive – and the feeding frenzy begins. Birds dive, sharks circle, and the netting crews competing for the ultimate catch. They brave shark-infested waters, navigate dangerous surf, and haul in heavy nets – all as tempers flare and tragedy hovers. This is a story of survival, tradition, and timing, set against the backdrop of a fragile coastal economy that lives and dies with the catch. Script: (Macfarlane) Every year, the greatest coastal migration on earth arrives in southern KwaZulu-Natal. (Macfarlane) Billions of sardines travel up from the Cape, following a narrow band of cold water that only occurs in winter. (Macfarlane) The predators are ready to feast. (Macfarlane) Those on land are ready, too. (Jace Govender) Let’s go! Pass the boat, let’s go! (Macfarlane) Each winter, traditional netters chase the shoal, hauling in sardines during the narrow window they're in these waters. It's a job that vanishes when the fish do. (Macfarlane) The risks - and the costs - are high. But so is the reward. (Macfarlane) A single net can bring in R100 000 worth of sardines a day. (Macfarlane) This is the sardine run and I’m joining the crews who chase fortune in every net they cast. (Macfarlane) It's early morning and, as the sun comes up, there's only one question that lingers on everyone's mind along the coastline: where are the sardines? (Macfarlane) One of the most well-known netters on the South Coast, Jace Govender scans the surf for any sign of sardines. He relies on his extensive network of spotters. (Jace Govender) Keep your eye on it. I’m coming there. I’m launching now, now, now. Guys, guys, guys. Come, let’s go! (Macfarlane) A spotter has seen a shoal close by. It’s game-on for Jace’s crew. He needs to launch his boat or lose out. (Macfarlane) This is where all the action begins, right. As exciting as it may seem, it's also the most dangerous part. (Macfarlane) It takes a seasoned boat skipper like Jace to make it through the surf. (Jace Govender Subtitles) This is a game. It’s a cat and mouse game. You have to run around, drive up and down. Some days you get lucky, some days you don’t. (Macfarlane) At first, it seems they’ve missed the shoal. Their luck is about to change. Time to lay the net. (Macfarlane) Once it’s laid, the real battle begins - pulling tonnes of net and fish back to shore. (Macfarlane Subtitles) Vans are getting stuck, people are falling over, it’s a mess. But it’s a wild and lovely mess. (Macfarlane) Jace and his crew have struck gold, in silver. (Macfarlane) Look! I caught my first sardine on the sardine run. (Macfarlane) How long have you been doing this for? (Jace Govender) All my life. I was born into it, I think, even before I was born, it was set for me to be a waterman. (Macfarlane) Is it dangerous? (Jace Govender) I think it's one of the most dangerous jobs in the world. You got the ocean to deal with. Two-tonne net, boat. Then you've got the sharks. (Macfarlane) The sharks? (Jace Govender) Yes, the big sharks. (Macfarlane) Just how dangerous was demonstrated last year when our producers filmed veteran netter Goolam Essack hauling his final net. (Goolam Essack Subtitles) I’m 74 now. I started as a 10-year-old boy. (Unknown) For 65 years. (Macfarlane) Tragically, Goolam’s boat capsized while netting and he suffered a fatal heart attack. (Jace Govender Subtitles) Goolam is late, but his family's still into it. His son, his daughter, everyone. Goolam married my cousin. So, we’re family. (Macfarlane) It’s a family affair. (Macfarlane) But there’s little time to dwell on his family’s loss. Jace says that the sardine run employs up to 5000 people, and he has a full net to sell. (Jace Govender) It's always a good day when you get the first net, because you’ll get the first buyers. So, you get the best price. The market can get flooded during the course of the day, but it also gives me a chance now to get a second net. (Macfarlane) Once the fish are caught, there’s no time to waste - buyers want them fresh. (Macfarlane) They’re packed into crates and sold, either to eat or as fishing bait. (Macfarlane) That’s where Tony Moon comes in. (Tony Moon) Hey! Bring all the fish here, guys! (Macfarlane) With more than 50 years’ experience behind him, he’s one of the South Coast’s biggest netters and sardine sellers. (Macfarlane) I see you are busy. It's like Tony's fish market. (Tony Moon) Ja. (Macfarlane) Do prices change throughout the day? (Tony Moon) Yes, yes, yes. (Macfarlane) Because I see, depending on… (Tony Moon) You see in the morning, if only one guy nets, we can get a good price. (Tony Moon) But when there's five netters netting and they’ve got full nets, then you know the guys are going to cut each and everybody's prices down. (Sardine Seller) R20 a dozen! Three dozen, R50! (Tony Moon) I started off here with R300, I went to R200 and now I'm selling R100. (Macfarlane) And just like that, the coast goes quiet - not a sardine in sight. But they’re still out there. And so are the sharks. Lots of them. (Macfarlane) The KwaZulu-Natal Sharks Board monitors shark activity along this coastline - especially during the sardine run. (Macfarlane) Matt Dicken is their head of research. (Matt Dicken) We monitor the sardines all the way from where they originate. And we track the movements up the coast to enable us to better predict the arrival of sardines so we can remove the bather protection gear, so we don't have mass captures of sharks and other animals in our gear. (Macfarlane) The Sharks Board manages shark nets and baited hooks known as drumlines around popular beaches, aimed at lowering the incidence of shark attacks. (Matt Dicken) So, when the gear comes out, the municipalities ban bathing. (Macfarlane) During this time, it seems that there's more sharks than normal. (Matt Dicken) The sardine run means a lot more sharks. When we talk about hundreds of thousands of tonnes of sardines, that obviously represents such an incredible food source not just for the sharks, but for a whole variety of predators. (Macfarlane) We just heard that there may be a catch happening a few kilometres down. So, we are going to drive there and see what we can find. Sardine run! (Macfarlane) This netting crew seems to be struggling with their catch. (Jonathan Stamatis) Just got a huge net of fish that we can't even pull it up the beach! (Macfarlane) Netter Demetri Stamatis is the conductor of this controlled chaos. (Demetri Stamatis) Let’s move down slowly! (Macfarlane) Driving the rhythm as his crew battles the net and the surf. (Demetri Stamatis) Pick the sinkers up! Let it out! (Macfarlane) This looks like a huge net. (Demetri Stamatis) It’s a big net today. We had to let a lot of fish go. I think that’s about 350 crates or so. (Macfarlane) Like Jace, Demetri has been doing this for a very long time. Decades ago, his father started netting from a rowboat. (Demetri Stamatis) I got involved five, six years old, running around with him and… Ja, it's been in our blood ever since. And so my kids have got involved. So, I've got my two boys with me. So, three generations. (Macfarlane) Three generations? (Demetri Stamatis What more could we ask for here? (Macfarlane) Your kids get in the water, they swim with the sharks. They’re pulling in those nets. Do you not sometimes sit there as a dad and think, “Oh, my God. I’m going to kill my son!” (Demetri Stamatis) I don’t know. My dad made me do it, so I'm not worried about them doing it. I’ve been there and done that. But I won’t let kids jump into the surf when it’s not right. (Macfarlane) Let's go, let's go, let's go! We’re making money, guys. (Demetri Stamatis) Okay, I need to go. (Macfarlane) All the best and thank you so much. Keep netting. (Macfarlane) This is so exciting. I mean, while we are doing the interview, calls are coming in. The market is fluctuating. Seeing it happen in real time is mind-blowing. (Macfarlane) Hold on, there’s a shark! (Macfarlane) So, this is what we’re talking about, right? This is how far these guys are willing to risk their lives. They swim with the sharks. (Macfarlane) It’s good news for Ryan Daly who tags and studies the sharks - including bronze whalers, dusky, spinner and blacktip sharks - drawn in by the sardine run. (Dr. Ryan Daly) So, every year the sharks follow up the sardines and there’s so many millions of sardines, we can't really track them. So, we use sharks as our indicators of where the sardines are. (Dr. Ryan Daly) The sharks are top predators and the sardines provide the biggest source of food for these predators on the whole coast. And so, sharks and sardines together play really important roles in the marine ecosystem. Sardines at the bottom of the food chain, sharks at the top of the food chain, keeping that balance. (Macfarlane) In the chaos of the beach, Ryan performs open shark surgery, inserting a tag while battling waves, shouting crews and curious onlookers. (Macfarlane) This year, over 20 sharks were caught in the nets in one day. (Macfarlane) How does that impact then the sort of ecological system there? (Dr. Ryan Daly) It's a really good sign, I think. So many sharks mean that there's a lot of sardines around. So, for me it's a good indicator that it's a strong run. (Macfarlane) Once the sharks are released from the net, are they safe? Do you check if it's good to release? (Dr. Ryan Daly) I've really experienced most of the netters caring about the sharks, making sure they're released safely. But we really don't know much about their survival after they get released. So, part of my question is to tag them after being caught in the nets to see if they do survive. (Macfarlane) These guys risk life and limb with the sharks for the sardine run, but they set it free... (Macfarlane) Ha, ha ,ha! Nice! (Macfarlane) Sharks are stuffing themselves with sardines. I want a taste of what they’re after. (Macfarlane) Are they fresh sardines? (Rani Judnarain) Absolutely. They were caught today. (Macfarlane) Did you catch them? (Jace Govender) Ja, you were there! That’s my work. (Macfarlane) I don’t mind eating food, but when it’s looking at me, it’s like, “Why are you doing this to me?” (Macfarlane) After all the action, a bit of satisfaction, right? (Jace Govender) This is the best form of protein. (Macfarlane) I guess, at the end of the day, after all the hard work has been done and you get to enjoy a sardine on the beach at sunset, the risk is worth it all.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A high-stakes, character-driven feature insert on South Africa's sardine run, told through the eyes of the netters who risk everything to chase a vanishing natural phenomenon.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: 1. Sardine Run Meets Human Drama This isn't just another wildlife story. It’s a high-adrenaline, character-driven human story set against one of the greatest natural spectacles on Earth. The sardines are the hook—but the people chasing them are the real story. 2. Exclusive, Real-Time Access The cameras are already rolling. We are embedded in the action with multiple crews and unprecedented access to the netters, skippers, and scientists. We've captured raw, real-time footage of chaos, danger, and victory—before anyone else. 3. Multi-Year, Multi-Perspective Coverage We bring a deep archive of sardine run footage: Inside bait balls in Port St Johns (freediving with sharks, dolphins, gannets) Netting chaos from 2020 to now (boats flipping, ropes snapping, crates flooding the beach) This year’s footage—sharks in nets, overturned vehicles, collapsing markets. No other team has this combination of past and present visual storytelling. 4. The Story Behind the Spectacle Most sardine run stories focus on the ocean. This story focuses on the people who depend on it—men and women gambling fuel, time, and safety for fish that might not come. It's blue-collar grit meets natural wonder. 5. Unfolding Economic Collapse The sardine run economy is imploding in real time. Prices dropped from R1000 to R300 per crate in days. Netters are giving away fish. The audience gets to witness the collapse of a coastal economy—as it happens. 6. Urgency of a Vanishing Event Scientists warn the sardine run may disappear by 2055 due to warming currents and ecological collapse. This may be one of the last great sardine runs—adding environmental urgency and journalistic relevance. 7. Diverse and Compelling Cast From "The Sardine Whisperer" to the family of a drowned legend… from a father-son boat crew to shark-tagging scientists… and a diver who swims into shark-infested surf—the cast is built for storytelling. 8. Visual Style Shot from the air, land, sea, and underwater, the project combines high-action GoPro, drone, underwater cinematography, and mobile footage. It's visually arresting, gritty, and immersive.
metadata.Summary: Every winter, billions of sardines migrate up the east coast of South Africa in one of the greatest wildlife spectacles on Earth. But the real story isn't just underwater—it's on the beach, in the boats, and behind the nets. On the Run is an immersive feature insert that captures the visceral chaos, the fierce rivalries, and the fragile economy built around the sardine run. It's a frontline story of fishermen who launch into pounding surf at first light, risking everything for a shoal that may never arrive. This is about more than fish. It's about survival, tradition, and timing. And it's already happening.
metadata.Further information: Current Status: The sardines arrived early this year. Nets are landing—some full of sardines, others full of sharks. Vehicles have rolled on the sand. Tempers are flaring. Our cameras are already rolling. The story is unfolding in real time. Our Focus: This insert will focus on the netters: approximately eight crews operating along the KwaZulu-Natal South Coast. These are small, competitive fishing teams who race against shifting currents, cold fronts, and each other to lay nets and get their catch to shore before the price crashes. Sardines sold for R1000 a crate on Saturday. By Monday, that dropped to R300. And now, the economic model is breaking down. Yesterday, Rustin, one of the young netters, opened his net and let the public take the sardines for free. The market has already collapsed, and the season has barely begun. For many crews, the maths simply doesn’t make sense anymore. The financial future of the sardine run is as uncertain as the fish themselves. We will place the presenter in the thick of it—launching with crews (only if the conditions are safe), hauling nets, walking the beach with skippers, and witnessing the chaos of a living, breathing economy built on the back of a fragile migration.
